title: Ketamine for depression
description: Ketamine, given as a single slow infusion under medical supervision, can lift depression quickly, unlike most treatments that take weeks; in this study, about half the people had responded a day later. People with depression were scanned at rest before an infusion and again a day later. In this episode brightness stands for how strongly an area is in step with the rest of the brain (its "global connectivity"), not for activity. In the first part it shows the difference from people without depression; in "What changed" it shows the change since before the infusion.
caveat: All findings come from one study of 18 people with depression that had not improved with two earlier antidepressants, and 25 people without depression. There was no placebo infusion. People had stopped antidepressants for only a week, so earlier medication may still have had effects. The study measures how much each area moves in step with the rest of the brain at rest, which is not the same as activity. "Lateral prefrontal cortex" is drawn on the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, an approximation. Differences between responders and non-responders were small, preliminary comparisons. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: Before treatment
phases.caption: Before the infusion, the prefrontal cortex was less in step with the rest of the brain than in people without depression, while the posterior cingulate and precuneus, part of the visual cortex and the cerebellum were more in step.

phases.name: One infusion
phases.caption: A single infusion, then about a day before the next scan. The brain is drawn at rest here.

citations.authors: Abdallah CG, Averill LA, Collins KA, Geha P, Schwartz J, Averill C, DeWilde KE, et al.
citations.title: Ketamine Treatment and Global Brain Connectivity in Major Depression.
citations.quote: MDD patients received a single infusion of ketamine and underwent repeated rs-fcMRI at 24 h posttreatment.

phases.name: What changed
phases.caption: A day later, the right lateral prefrontal cortex is more in step with the rest of the brain than before, and the left cerebellum less. Compared with people who did not respond, responders showed larger increases in the right lateral prefrontal cortex and the left anterior insula.

citations.authors: Abdallah CG, Averill LA, Collins KA, Geha P, Schwartz J, Averill C, DeWilde KE, et al.
citations.title: Ketamine Treatment and Global Brain Connectivity in Major Depression.
citations.quote: MDD patients received a single infusion of ketamine and underwent repeated rs-fcMRI at 24 h posttreatment.

phases.name: What stayed the same
phases.caption: A day later, the posterior cingulate, precuneus and visual areas no longer differed from people without depression, though they did not change significantly. How long the change lasts, and whether it explains the improvement, was not shown.

order.rationale: This last part is a summary of what the studies did not find or did not measure, not a later point in time.

regions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex was less in step with the rest of the brain than in people without depression before the infusion; a day after it, the right lateral prefrontal cortex was more in step, in one study.
